title: Converting currencies
objectives: Convert money with a quoted exchange rate and with its inverse
Measure a profit in pounds when prices move in another currency

screens.prose: At a bureau, £1 buys €1.16. The line shows what each amount of pounds buys. You change £300 for a trip.
screens.question: How many euros do you get for £300?

hints.text: How many euros does each pound buy?
£100 buys €116, so £300 buys three times as much.
Multiply £300 by 1.16.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each pound buys €1.16, so multiply.

byKey.divided: You divided by 1.16. Each pound buys more than one euro, so you should get more euros than pounds.
byKey.added: You added the rate to £300. The rate is per pound, so it multiplies every pound.

explain.text: Each of your 300 pounds buys €1.16, so you get 300 × 1.16 = €348. It is the same line as the recipes: euros $= 1.16 \times$ pounds, through (0, 0).

screens.prose: Now go the other way. Drag the point along the line and watch both amounts change.
screens.question: How many pounds do you need to get €580? Drag the point to show it.

hints.text: Stop when the euro amount reads 580.
The answer is fewer pounds than 580, because each pound buys more than €1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag until the label reads €580.

byKey.multiplied: At about £670 you would get about €777. You multiplied 580 by 1.16, but you are going from euros back to pounds.
byKey.same: £580 buys more than €580, because each pound buys €1.16.

explain.text: The point reads €580 at £500, since 500 × 1.16 = 580. Going from euros back to pounds, we divide: 580 ÷ 1.16 = 500.

screens.prose: The **exchange rate** €1.16 per £1 is a rate, like a price per gram. Its **inverse** is the same rate the other way round: pounds per euro.
screens.question: How many pounds does €1 buy? Give 4 decimal places.

widget.label: Pounds per euro
widget.accept: £0.8621, or any value within 0.0005 of it

hints.text: Which amount of pounds buys exactly €1?
£1 buys €1.16, so €1 costs less than £1.
Divide 1 by 1.16.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 1 by the rate.

byKey.same: That is the rate as quoted, euros per pound. The inverse turns it round: pounds per euro.
byKey.subtract: You took 0.16 off 1. Turning a rate round divides: 1 ÷ 1.16, which is not 1 − 0.16.
byKey.gap: That is the gap between €1.16 and €1. The inverse is 1 ÷ 1.16.

explain.text: €1 costs 1 ÷ 1.16 ≈ £0.8621. Check: 0.8621 × 1.16 ≈ 1.0000. A rate and its inverse multiply to 1, because they describe the same swap.

screens.prose: A real bureau quotes two rates. It sells you euros at €1.12 per £1. It buys euros back at €1.21 per £1. You change £500, spend nothing, then change it all back.
screens.question: How many pounds do you end with?

hints.text: Do the two swaps one at a time.
First £500 × 1.12 gives your euros. Coming back, divide by 1.21.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Buy euros at 1.12, then divide by 1.21 to come back.

byKey.same: You assumed the swap undoes itself. The bureau uses a worse rate each way, so you lose.
byKey.multiplied-back: You multiplied by 1.21 coming back. Euros to pounds divides by the rate.
byKey.one-rate: You used one rate both ways. The bureau gives €1.12 going out and wants €1.21 for each £1 coming back.

explain.text: £500 × 1.12 = €560. Coming back, each £1 costs €1.21, so you get 560 ÷ 1.21 ≈ £462.81. The gap between the two rates, the spread, cost you £37.19.

screens.prose: Rates can be chained. A bank's screen shows these two rates.
screens.question: How many yen does £1 buy, going through euros?

hints.text: First turn £1 into euros.
£1 gives €1.16, and every euro gives ¥160.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Change pounds to euros, then every euro to yen.

byKey.divided: You divided 160 by 1.16. Each pound gives more than one euro, so it gives more than ¥160.
byKey.added: You added the two rates. Each of the 1.16 euros turns into ¥160, so multiply.

explain.text: £1 gives €1.16, and each of those euros gives ¥160. So £1 gives 1.16 × 160 = ¥185.60. Chained rates multiply.

screens.prose: A trading screen quotes the rate the other way: €1 costs £0.85. A colleague converts £1,000 by multiplying: £1,000 × 0.85 = €850.
screens.question: How many euros does £1,000 really buy?

options.why: You multiplied by the pounds-per-euro rate. That turns euros into pounds, so you went the wrong way.
You added the 15p gap, as if the inverse of 0.85 were 1.15. It is 1 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 1.1765.
You treated a pound and a euro as equal. The quote says €1 costs less than £1.

hints.text: Is a euro worth more or less than a pound here?
Each euro costs £0.85, so £1,000 buys more than 1,000 euros.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many £0.85 euros fit into £1,000.

byKey.times: You multiplied by the pounds-per-euro rate. That turns euros into pounds, not pounds into euros.

explain.text: Each euro costs £0.85, so £1,000 buys 1,000 ÷ 0.85 ≈ €1,176.47. Multiplying gives fewer euros than pounds, which the quote rules out. Always check which currency the rate is per.

screens.prose: Call $r$ the euros per pound. Then $$\text{euros} = r \times \text{pounds}, \qquad \text{pounds} = \frac{\text{euros}}{r}$$ The inverse rate is $\dfrac{1}{r}$ pounds per euro. Both rates describe the same line.
screens.question: A rate is €1.25 per £1. What is the inverse rate, in pounds per euro?

options.why: You took 0.25 off 1. The inverse divides: 1 ÷ 1.25 = 0.80.
That keeps the number and swaps the units. It would make a euro worth more than a pound, the wrong way round.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 1 by the rate.

explain.text: The inverse of 1.25 is 1 ÷ 1.25 = 0.80. Check: 0.80 × 1.25 = 1. A rate times its inverse is always 1.

screens.prose: Change £250 into yen through euros, then find the single pound-to-yen rate. Use £1 = €1.16 and €1 = ¥160.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $250 \times 185.6 = 46{,}400$, the single rate gives the same yen

hints.text: What must you have before you can buy yen?
Pounds become euros first, then euros become yen.
Euros, then yen, then the combined rate, then the check.

feedback.correct: Two swaps, one combined rate, one check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the money: pounds, then euros, then yen.

byKey.yen: You need the €290 before you can turn it into yen.
byKey.check: The check uses the combined rate, so that rate comes first.

explain.text: You changed £250 to €290, then €290 to ¥46,400. Combining the rates gives ¥185.60 per pound, and 250 × 185.6 gives the same ¥46,400.

screens.prose: You buy 200 shares of a German company at €58.00 each, when £1 = €1.16. Later you sell at €63.80 each, when £1 = €1.21.
screens.question: What is your profit in pounds?

hints.text: Convert the cost and the proceeds into pounds, each at its own rate.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Convert each amount at the rate on its own day.

byKey.old-rate: You kept the buying rate for the sale. The pound strengthened, so each euro buys fewer pounds.
byKey.euro-profit: That is the profit in euros. Convert the cost and the proceeds into pounds first.
byKey.multiplied: You multiplied euros by the rates. Euros to pounds divides by the euros-per-pound rate.

explain.text: The shares cost €11,600 ÷ 1.16 = £10,000. They sold for €12,760 ÷ 1.21 ≈ £10,545.45. The share rose 10% in euros, but the stronger pound cut your gain to about 5.5%.

ideas: An exchange rate is a rate: euros per pound. Multiply to go with it, divide to go against it.
The inverse rate is $1/r$, never $1 - (r - 1)$. A rate times its inverse is 1.
Chained rates multiply. A buy rate and a sell rate differ, and the spread is a cost.

formula.name: Currency conversion
formula.note: Check which currency the quote is per before you multiply.

summary.trap: A quote of £0.85 per euro is not €0.85 per pound. Multiplying by the wrong-way rate sends you the wrong way.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Euros to pounds divides by the rate.

byKey.multiplied: You multiplied by 1.16. That turns pounds into euros, the other way.

quiz.question: What is ¥1 worth in pence? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Share 100p between 190 yen.

byKey.same: That is the rate as quoted. One yen is worth far less than a penny.
byKey.pounds: That is the value in pounds. Multiply by 100 for pence.

explain.text: £1 is 100p, and it buys ¥190. So ¥1 is worth 100 ÷ 190 ≈ 0.53p.

quiz.prose: A bureau sells euros at €1.10 per £1 and buys them back at €1.22 per £1. You change £200 and then change it all back.
quiz.question: How much do you lose, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Do the two swaps one at a time.

byKey.rate-gap: You multiplied £200 by the 0.12 gap between the rates. Do each swap: €220, then 220 ÷ 1.22.
byKey.none: You assumed the swaps cancel. The bureau uses a worse rate each way.

explain.text: £200 × 1.10 = €220. Back again, 220 ÷ 1.22 ≈ £180.33. You lose about £19.67 to the spread.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Both rates start from £1, so compare them.

byKey.multiplied: You multiplied the rates. €1.16 and ¥190 are both worth £1, so €1 buys 190 ÷ 1.16 yen.

explain.text: €1.16 and ¥190 are both worth £1, so they are worth the same. One euro is worth 190 ÷ 1.16 ≈ ¥163.79.
